principle: Directional instructions must be relational, not ambiguous left/right
definition: Always use the creator's own left and right as they face the phone: 'the window on your left', 'turn a little to your right'. Never say camera-left or camera-right, because left and right flip once the phone and the creator face each other. Then say where the light sits relative to the face, not just where it is in the room: for example 'keep the window on your left, a little in front of you and slightly above your eyes, and turn your face a little toward it'. Outdoors, also give the sun's direction and height from the creator when known (in front of you, behind your left shoulder, high overhead).

principle: Apparent source size determines softness, not source type
definition: A source's softness depends on its apparent size relative to the subject, not what it 'is' -- the sun is physically enormous but so distant it acts as a small hard source; a large nearby window or bounce surface appears larger and produces softer shadows. A curtain can turn a small bright opening into a broad diffuse source.

principle: Inverse-square falloff (point sources) vs. large soft sources
definition: For a point-like source, doubling the distance yields about one-quarter the illuminance (a two-stop loss). Large soft sources behave differently at close range -- ASC measurements show a gentler initial falloff. Do not apply the point-source rule blindly to a large softbox or close window.
further_reading: creator_lighting_positioning_research.md, citing ASC 'Revisiting and Updating Inverse-Square Law'

principle: Camera distance, not focal length, changes facial perspective
definition: Camera-to-subject distance changes perspective (how features appear relative to each other); focal length mainly changes field of view. A 'compressed' telephoto look results from moving farther away and reframing with a longer lens -- a longer lens does not itself compress perspective if camera position is unchanged.

principle: Clock time is not a sun direction
definition: Solar noon is not necessarily clock noon; sun azimuth/elevation must be derived from location, date, and time (e.g. via NOAA's solar calculator), not assumed from the clock alone. Do not plan a shot around a clock time alone; check where the sun is for your place and date.
further_reading: creator_lighting_positioning_research.md, citing NOAA Solar Position Calculator

situation: You are squinting, or direct sun is throwing hard, uncomfortable shadows on your face
first_move: Move into continuous shade, or turn your body away from the direct sun, before you change exposure.
why: Squinting and hard sun shadows come from where the light is; changing brightness on the phone does not remove them.

situation: Your face is dark against a bright window or sky
first_move: Change where the phone points or what is behind you so the bright window or sky is not behind your head, or add light on your face (a lamp, or a white card bouncing light back). Do not just darken the whole picture.
why: Darkening the whole frame to save the bright window leaves your face too dark to use; fixing the positions keeps both readable.

situation: The background behind you is distracting
first_move: Move the phone or move yourself before you zoom in or switch lenses.
why: Moving changes what is behind you directly, and the camera's distance from you, not the zoom, is what changes how your face looks.

situation: The main light is directly overhead (ceiling light or high sun)
first_move: Move yourself or the light, or bounce light up from low in front of you with a white card or sheet. Tilting or lowering the phone is not a lighting fix.
why: The dark eye-socket and nose shadows come from where the light sits; a different camera angle only shows them differently.

situation: Close-up shot on a very wide camera held close to your face
first_move: Move the phone farther away and use the main 1x camera, or a real optical telephoto if your phone has one; keep your face near the centre and reframe.
why: Being very close makes the nearest features, like the nose, look bigger than they are; a wide camera is only what lets you get that close -- the distance changes the face, not the lens.

situation: The light is too hard, or too soft and flat
first_move: If it is too hard, make the light bigger: diffuse it through a sheer curtain, bounce it off a pale wall, or move into shade. If it is too soft and flat, reduce the fill or use a smaller main light placed more to the side.
why: Softness depends on how big the light looks from your face: a bigger source gives softer shadows, a smaller or more distant one gives harder shadows.

situation: Lights of different colours are falling on your face
first_move: Pick one light as your face light, switch the others off or keep them only in the background, and set white balance for that face light.
why: One white-balance setting cannot make two differently coloured lights look neutral at the same time.

situation: Wide shot that shows the whole room or location
first_move: Check the entire frame -- every light, window and background area -- not just your face.
why: A fix that works for your face may not cover the room behind you once the whole space is in the shot.

situation: You are moving on camera in low light
first_move: Add a steady, continuous light and keep the phone stable before relying on Night mode.
why: Night mode can take several seconds per capture and works best with a steady phone, so movement blurs.

setup: A soft main light 30 to 45 degrees to one side of your face and slightly above your eyes, only a little fill on the other side, your face turned slightly toward the light, the phone steady at eye level, and a background a little darker than you or about the same, with one controlled lamp in it.
check: Both eyes stay visible and your skin keeps its texture. Avoid a very bright window, strongly coloured background LEDs, and light that comes only from overhead. How much fill to use depends on your room.
fits_categories: Influora's suggestion, not from the guide: Personal finance, Education and Tech & gadgets explainers, and business talk. The guide's label: serious educational/business/finance/technology.
limits: The exact angle is a starting point to test, not a law.

setup: Use the window or light that is already in the room as your main light so it looks natural there, let meaningful parts of your real space show, and if your face looks flat put something dark (a dark cloth or the darker side of the room) on the side away from the light to keep shape.
check: The light should still make sense for the room. Do not over-light a naturally dim room if that clashes with what you are talking about.
fits_categories: Influora's suggestion, not from the guide: expert and founder-style talks where your real space matters, for example in Education, Personal finance or Tech & gadgets. The guide's label: documentary/expert/founder.

setup: A broad light from in front of you and a little to one side (a window, or open shade outdoors), with you sitting close to it, soft shadows, a neutral-to-warm feel only if a warm light in the scene explains it, and a background that is tidy but lived-in.
check: Avoid completely flat front light if you want some depth. In product demos, make sure your hands and the product sit in the same light as your face.
fits_categories: Influora's suggestion, not from the guide: Beauty & skincare, Lifestyle, Food and Fashion, and product demos. The guide's label: friendly/natural/lifestyle/UGC.

setup: A bright, controlled background and a brightly lit you, with few hard dark shadows.
check: The background may need its own light or exposure. Watch that the brightest parts of your skin do not turn pure white.
fits_categories: Influora's suggestion, not from the guide: bright, airy content such as Beauty & skincare, Wellness or Lifestyle. The guide's label: high-key.

setup: Main light from the side or edge, little fill, a darker background, and something dark on the shadow side of your face (negative fill).
check: Keep detail in the shadows wherever information matters. Do not blow out the lit cheek or lose the far eye by accident.
fits_categories: Influora's suggestion, not from the guide: dramatic moments and storytelling segments, for example in Comedy & entertainment or Gaming; avoid it for beauty close-ups unless the shadow side is lifted with fill. The guide's label: low-key/dramatic.

setup: A bright background or light behind you, the phone exposed for that bright background, and no light on your face.
check: Use a clean outline against the bright area, and make it clear the missing face detail is on purpose.
fits_categories: Influora's suggestion, not from the guide: mood shots, sunset openers and transitions, for example in Travel or Lifestyle; not for talking-to-camera explainers where your face must be seen. The guide's label: silhouette.

recommendation: Use the window as your face light. Switch the lamp off, or move it behind you as a warm lamp in the background. If your phone allows it, lock white balance on your face and the background lamp can stay warm if you like the look; otherwise switch the lamp off.

Use the warm bulb (or a window) for your face and switch the ceiling LED off; if the ceiling light is the only light you have, switch off the warm bulb and bounce light up onto your face with a white card or sheet held low in front of you.
Use the brighter window as your face light, and curtain or cover the other one if it throws shadows in a different direction.

mix: Phone auto white balance shifts during the take
recommendation: Lock or set white balance if your phone allows it. If it does not, cut down the competing light colours and do not walk through areas lit by different colours during the shot.
Lock white balance if your phone allows it, so your shots match, or change it deliberately once between scenes. Add a steady face light as the daylight drops.

instruction: Decide between three looks: sun on your face, sun behind one shoulder as a rim of light, or a silhouette. If the sun is on your face, keep it out of your eyes so you do not squint. If it is behind you as a rim, face toward the open sky or a white card on the phone's side of you.
limits: Timing depends on your location and date, not the clock; recheck your face and background every few minutes as the sun drops.

instruction: Shift the phone a little so the sun itself is not in line with the lens, unless you want flare or a silhouette. If the rim of light disappears, reframe against a darker background.
limits: Timing depends on your location and date, not the clock; recheck your face and background every few minutes as the sun drops.

instruction: Bring a soft light closer to your face or move to a brighter spot. Do not assume the phone will keep a clean picture on its own -- expect grain and motion blur.

instruction: Keep the phone steady, use the main camera, light your face from near the phone, and let distant lamps and signs become points of light in the background.

main_risk: It does not beat distance or echo; needs a furry cover outdoors; works only at close conversation range.

decision_tree: First ask: can it be switched off for 30-90 seconds? If yes, switch it off, record, then record 15-30 seconds of the room with it running normally. If it must run: use a lav or wireless transmitter 20-30 cm from the mouth (never fight a loud fan with a phone 1-2 m away), and keep the creator out of the direct airflow and out of line with the fan or AC outlet.

noise_source: Traffic that comes and goes (horn, bus, construction)
decision_tree: Stop speaking, hold the framing, wait, then repeat the whole sentence -- do not talk through a horn and expect it to be fixed later.

Stand on the sheltered side of a building or wall, use a close lav with a furry windscreen, keep the traffic behind the creator only if its air does not reach the mic, and keep takes short. If the voice is still drowned, film the picture without speech and record the voiceover indoors.

Music is both a rights problem and a problem for hearing the words. A close mic helps the voice but cannot fully remove nearby voices or music -- ask for the music to be turned down, change tables, or record the intro somewhere else; use the place for B-roll without speech.

Light: close mic with a foam cover, and turn the body so the air does not hit the mic openings directly. Moderate: furry windshield, use a wall, building or vehicle as a barrier, keep speech short. Strong or gusting: do not rely on the phone mic or its noise cancelling -- move behind a solid barrier, record without speech and add a voiceover, or shoot another day.

Put the creator and the mic near soft things (curtains, sofa, bedding, rugs) rather than a bare wall, window or corner; keep the mouth 0.5-1 m from a bare wall. Bathrooms, kitchens and empty halls are for voiceover or a close lav only.

noise_source: Indian home (TV, mixer, cooker, exhaust, fridge)
decision_tree: Pause the TV, mixer, pressure cooker, exhaust fan, washing machine and nearby phone alerts while speaking. Close a street-facing window or door for road noise, then check whether the room needs the AC or fan for heat. Vendors, dogs, children and prayer bells come and go -- hold and retake. Fridge compressor: move the mic farther from the fridge (not just the camera).

placement: Centre of the upper chest, 20-30 cm below the mouth; run the cable under the shirt with a loop taped so a tug does not pull the mic.
avoid: Necklaces, beard or hair, and fabric rubbing on the transmitter.

placement: Mount it on a stable blouse or saree layer near the upper chest, cushioned with tape or a cover; test while moving.
avoid: Covering the mic tightly with the dupatta, or pinning it to an edge that moves.

placement: On the upper placket or an inside layer, cushioned from the fabric.
avoid: The dupatta edge or jewellery touching it.

likely_cause: The mic is too far, or the phone is filming wide from far away.
fix: A close lav, or bring the camera closer to the speaker.

likely_cause: A hard room plus a distant mic.
ten_second_test: Clap or speak at 1 m, then at 20 cm from the mic.
fix: Add soft furnishing or move rooms; bring the mic close.

likely_cause: Cloth, the case or a hand is blocking the mic.
ten_second_test: Uncover and clean the mic opening, then repeat.
fix: Reposition it; never seal the mic in.

likely_cause: AC, fan or an electrical source.
ten_second_test: Switch the source off briefly and listen.
fix: Switch it off, move away, or use a close mic; keep the original recording.

ten_second_test: Face each direction of the wind and listen.
fix: Furry windscreen, a barrier, and the body as a shield.

rule: Cut by default
guidance: When the creator moves and the sound and light change, two clean clips usually work better than one continuous talking take. Finish the thought in the controlled spot, record a silent walking shot or B-roll as the bridge, and start talking again once exposure, white balance and sound have settled at the new spot. Walk and talk continuously only when all of these hold: a close wireless mic, a steady route, wind and noise under control, and a real visual reason to keep walking.

rule: Quiet spot to noisy spot
guidance: Finish the important sentence indoors. Say a bridging line ("let's step outside"), then cut or show a silent door or walking shot. At the new spot, record 5 seconds of the surroundings, let the exposure settle, and start a new sentence with a close lav and a furry cover. Prefer a voiceover if the traffic competes with the words.

rule: Noisy spot to quiet spot
guidance: Do not let the phone's automatic level and exposure changes happen while you talk. End the part in the noisy spot, film a wide shot of the place with no speech, then at the quiet spot pause 2-3 seconds, check the mic position and level, and start again. Keep a little of the location sound under the edit so the cut does not sound unnaturally silent.

rule: Exposure and white balance across the move
guidance: Dark to bright (indoors to sun): walk first, stop in open shade if you can, and wait for the auto exposure to settle before speaking; lock exposure and focus (AE/AF lock) only once the face looks right -- an exposure locked indoors blows out outdoors. Bright to dark: stop and let the phone raise the exposure and refocus; do not push a walking, talking take through the change. Daylight to warm indoor light: keep one main light source; lock white balance only for takes in the same light.

rule: Direction of travel and the 180-degree line
guidance: Pick the direction the creator moves across the frame in the first shot and keep it in the next shot, unless you show a clear reset (a doorway, a wide shot of the place, a clear turn). For two people talking, keep every camera on one side of the line between them -- crossing it flips where they look. A talking-head clip does not need a strict 180-degree line, but the body direction, where the eyes look and the side the main light comes from should match across a cut unless the change is on purpose.

camera_setup: Eye height, 1x, ending on a medium or wide shot.
audio: Lav; start talking only once close, or use a voiceover.
light_transition: Walk from shade to a marked spot with controlled light; cut when you stop.

recommended_solution: Use the close lav; do a 10-second headphone test; switch off or avoid the noise source where possible; record a voiceover if the speech is still drowned.

recommended_solution: Close wireless lav with a furry windscreen; shield it with the body or a building; keep takes short; voiceover if the speech is still drowned.

environment: Indoors, moving from the bedroom to the living room.
microphone: Wired lav, in the same position before and after the cut.
camera_setup: Eye height, 1x, same direction of travel across the frame, cut with a silent walking shot.
audio_problem: The sound and the light change with the room.
recommended_solution: Finish talking before the cut, use a silent walking shot as the bridge, and wait for exposure, white balance and sound to settle in the new room before talking again; keep the direction of travel, the mic position and the side the main light comes from the same.

label: ECU / extreme close-up
visible_area: A facial feature, eyes, or a small detail
gives_viewer: Fine expression or object detail; little context

label: CU / close-up
visible_area: Most/all of the face, often head cropped

label: MS / medium
gives_viewer: Gesture and some environment; useful for dialogue/action

label: FS / full
visible_area: Head to toe, subject relatively large
gives_viewer: Whole-body action while retaining some setting

label: LS / wide / long
visible_area: Head to toe or a smaller figure with more environment
gives_viewer: Establishes place, scale, distance, or the subject's relation to the setting
note: These labels do not prescribe a focal length or stand-off distance — boundaries overlap across schools; use the visible crop as the definition.

movement: Static/locked frame
use_when: The action itself is the point — speaking, sitting, holding a product steady, demonstrating in a stable composition
why: Preserves precise headroom, text space, and product readability

movement: Pan (rotation, not translation)
use_when: Follow someone crossing the frame or reveal a destination outside the initial frame
why: Rotates from a fixed position; if staying beside the subject is the goal, physically track instead of panning

movement: Push-in / pull-out (physical translation, not zoom)
use_when: Emphasize a face/product (push) or reveal context (pull)
why: A physical push changes perspective and foreground/background relationships; a zoom only changes focal length and does NOT produce the same effect — keep the move slow and short for simple creator video

movement: Tracking/truck
use_when: Following a walking subject's route, or when the environment should pass behind the creator
why: Moves parallel with the subject to hold roughly the same distance/size while background shifts

movement: Handheld
use_when: A subjective, urgent, or informal feel is wanted
why: Fast and close, can feel immediate/documentary; visible instability can distract — lock off or stabilize for polished product demos or instructional close-ups instead

movement: Whip pan
use_when: A fast transition or reveal beat
why: Produces motion blur that can bridge a transition, but needs an intentional start and target or the result is just an unreadable smear

principle: Read the light before choosing the mark
definition: The first shot-planning question is not 'where is the ring light' but 'what source is already shaping the face, product, and background.' Inspect the face from camera-side and window-side, note the bright side, shadow side, and cast-shadow direction, before placing the subject and camera.

principle: Shadow visibility is an intent test, not a defect
definition: A source's position determines shadow direction, angle, and length. Removing every shadow can remove texture and depth. Ask: does this shadow clarify shape, create depth/mood, or hide information the viewer needs?

principle: Mixed color sources are not inherently wrong
definition: Indoor window light, ceiling fixtures, lamps, and screens commonly differ in color temperature (candlelight ~2700K, daylight ~5600K). A warm practical against cooler daylight can read as a believable room or deliberate contrast. It becomes distracting only when the face/product is split by incompatible casts unintentionally, or a visible source doesn't seem to explain the illumination.

A large apparent source (via diffusion) makes softer shadows; the lit diffusion becomes the effective source. More diffusion can cost light intensity and shift color. Diffusion cannot rescue a badly placed key light.

instruction: Identify the verb (walk/show/move/sit), the item or information that must be visible, and whether the action should be shown continuously or can cut.

step: Fix the location and light geometry
instruction: Name the doorway/window/chair/tabletop/path; state where the source is relative to subject and camera, and whether it's direct, soft, mixed, or changing.

State the camera's physical location, lens-facing direction, and height relative to the final performance. Eye-level is a conversational starting point; raise/lower only to show a needed surface, product, or viewpoint.

step: Block subject start, path and destination
instruction: Use clear marks ('start by doorway, cross left-to-right, stop beside window, turn face 30 deg toward light'). Define whether the creator exits the initial frame or stays visible throughout.
Use locked-off, pan, tilt, push, track, or handheld only if it serves the action or reveal. Specify direction and end position; blocking often solves a shot more simply than adding camera motion.

step: Describe the frame at beginning and end
instruction: Name shot size, visible body parts, headroom intention, screen position, lead room, background, and product position for both the start and end of the move.
Assign text to the actual negative space left by subject/hand/product, not a generic side. Then test against platform interface/caption overlays, since those vary by app and change over time.
Have the creator reach the mark, complete the action, hold the final pose/product for a short beat, and leave the camera settled before cutting.

definition: Perspective (apparent size/spacing of objects at different distances) depends on camera VIEWPOINT/distance, not focal length. At the same viewpoint, changing focal length mainly changes which part of the scene is included. The 'telephoto compression' look results from moving the camera farther away to keep the subject the same size, not from the lens itself. Move the camera farther from the face to reduce close-viewpoint exaggeration; use lens choice to recover the desired framing — zoom alone does not 'fix' distortion.
further_reading: Smartphone_camera__lens__distance_and_backgrounds.md, citing a peer-reviewed picture-perception study and MIT image-formation lecture notes

principle: Zoom labels (0.5x/1x/2x/3x) are framing controls, not a shared industry promise
definition: What camera/processing actually happens behind a zoom label depends on the model, lighting, resolution, stabilization setting, and camera app — it may select an ultrawide/main/telephoto module, crop a high-res sensor, or combine optical+computational processing. Do not equate '0.5x' or '3x' with one precise equivalent focal length or a guaranteed optical telephoto on every phone.
further_reading: Smartphone_camera__lens__distance_and_backgrounds.md, citing Samsung Galaxy S24 camera documentation

principle: Subject-to-background separation test (not a fixed distance rule)
definition: There is no camera-maker or cinematography standard for a universal phone-to-wall distance. As a starting TEST (not an evidence-based threshold), try 0.6-1.5m (2-5ft) of separation from a nearby wall when the room allows, then check for a hard wall shadow, an object appearing to grow from the head, and whether the face is distinct from the background.

rule: Use a head-and-shoulders or chest-up frame; keep the face unobstructed and large enough to read expressions.
rationale: Portrait creator guidance favors close head-and-shoulders framing for self-shot content; close-ups emphasize facial expression.

rule: Frame the face and the working hand together when both are necessary to understand the step; change to a tighter detail shot for precision work.
rationale: A beauty creator describes moving closer for precise eye work, while shot-size guidance distinguishes expressive close-ups from wider context. Treat this as a practical shot-plan choice, not a universal tested framing.

rule: Show the creator first, then give the product its own close detail shot; do not make a small package compete with the face in one crowded frame.
rationale: Product demonstrations are clearer when key features are shown in close-up; a face-plus-product split sequence preserves both demonstration and human context.

rule: Hold the label toward camera beside the face, at a distance where both remain legible, and check focus before recording the take.
rationale: This is an operational recommendation derived from product-feature visibility and the camera maker's close-up-demo guidance; exact hand position varies with package and lens.

scenario: Eye, lip, or skin texture demonstration
rule: Use a dedicated close-up for the treated area; keep explanatory text off the feature being demonstrated.
rationale: Close shots direct attention to a specific feature, and instructional callouts should clarify rather than cover the underlying visual information.

scenario: Creator applies makeup using a mirror
rule: Place the mirror where the creator can work naturally without repeatedly leaving the composed frame; capture an insert if precision requires moving closer.
rationale: A creator's first-person setup documents mirror viewing and moving out of frame for precision. It is a useful anecdote, not a measured general rule.

scenario: Talking head with a product claim or step label
rule: Put short text in the visually quieter side of the frame, not over eyes, skin detail, or the hand applying product.
rationale: Negative space can direct attention; screen annotations should not cover or overpower key content. Recheck that the chosen side does not collide with the target app's live UI.

rule: Keep camera angle, subject scale, and pose consistent between comparison states; use a clean cut or clearly labeled split rather than shifting the face position.
rationale: Maintaining comparable framing makes the visual difference easier to judge; this is a practical comparison-design recommendation, not a directly tested creator outcome.

rule: Choose a frame wide enough to include the hair section and both hands involved; move to a close insert for small tool or texture details.
rationale: Medium views retain action/body context while close-ups isolate details. Let the action, rather than a fixed crop, determine the useful frame.

rule: Favor direct-to-lens eye contact for audience address; reserve a deliberate off-camera look for a conversational or reflective beat.
rationale: Interview cinematography distinguishes direct audience address from an off-camera conversational eyeline; the choice communicates different relationships with viewers.

rule: Use a full-length frame when head-to-toe silhouette and styling are the point; verify shoes and garment hems stay inside the picture during movement.
rationale: A long/full shot shows the whole subject and context; checking the action's full extent is a practical crop safeguard.

rule: Add a close insert of the detail rather than asking a full-body view to communicate small texture or hardware.
rationale: Close-ups isolate one element and product-video instruction recommends close-ups of distinguishing specifications.

rule: Leave visible space in the direction of travel and keep the intended walking path inside the vertical frame.
rationale: Lead room gives a moving subject visual destination; full-frame orientation requires checking motion at both ends of the take.

scenario: Creator stands off-center for outfit text
rule: Place the creator on one side and a concise outfit label in the opposite uncluttered space; reverse the arrangement if the garment or app UI makes that side busy.
rationale: Thirds and negative space support off-center composition; no source establishes a universal side for text across apps.

rule: Compose so the reflection, outfit edges, and relevant styling details are visible; remove distracting room objects from the mirror background where possible.
rationale: A reflection can justify centered/symmetrical composition; distracting elements weaken visual clarity.

rule: Keep the subject's landing position and scale similar on both sides of a match transition, unless the change in scale is intentionally part of the reveal.
rationale: Canon creator guidance recommends purposeful, consistent transitions; matching positions is a practical editing convention rather than an empirical threshold.

rule: Use a medium-long or full-body view that shows the garment moving against enough background to separate its outline.
rationale: Knee-up to full shots show movement and body language; subject-background separation helps a silhouette read.

rule: Use a chest-up frame for explanation, then cut to the relevant full outfit or detail instead of keeping one frame for every beat.
rationale: Shot size conveys different information: tighter views retain expression; wider views show clothing and context.

rule: Use a location-establishing view before tighter outfit coverage; keep background landmarks supportive rather than competing with the clothing.
rationale: Wide/medium views establish setting and tighter shots emphasize subject detail; a busy background can distract.

rule: Frame the complete range of the demonstrated movement, including the lowest or widest position, before recording the working set.
rationale: Movement coverage should preserve necessary body/action context; workout production guidance stresses shot planning and framing/composition, while this range check is a practical safety-of-coverage test.

rule: Use a medium or medium-close frame for the spoken cue, then show the full movement in a wider view.
rationale: Medium framing supports dialogue and body language; the wider shot conveys the whole exercise action.

scenario: Showing a joint or grip correction
rule: Use a close insert only to point out the relevant joint, hand, or equipment position, and follow it with a full-context demonstration.
rationale: Close-ups make specific details legible, while a wider shot re-establishes the complete action; this sequencing is a practical teaching recommendation.

scenario: Standing workout in a small room
rule: Move the camera back or use a wider field of view until the whole movement fits; avoid relying on a tight talking-head crop for a movement lesson.
rationale: Long/full shots include complete body and environment; focal length changes field of view, so validate framing on the actual phone/lens.

rule: Keep the implement and the body part using it visible together during the key action.
rationale: The instructional image must show the subject and relevant action; medium/wide framing carries more body/action information than a face close-up.

rule: Place rep/form labels in clear background space and away from the body alignment being taught.
rationale: Negative space can carry text, but screen annotations should not cover the underlying instructional information.

rule: Leave room on both sides if the exercise moves both ways; do not compose only for the starting pose.
rationale: Shot planning should anticipate action rather than freeze on the initial composition; full-body movement requires adequate action space.

rule: Alternate an establishing gym view, a full-body action view, and selected detail inserts; use each shot for a distinct piece of information.
rationale: Workout guides recommend planning segments and camera angles; shot variety is a creator-education practice, not a validated engagement formula.

scenario: Solo creator moving away from a fixed phone
rule: Test the full movement and use the actual platform preview; adjust camera distance or frame if the subject leaves the view.
rationale: Different actions require planned coverage; a test is preferable to guessing a universal distance.

scenario: Exercise content in a shared gym
rule: Compose tightly enough to focus on the demonstrating creator and avoid unintentionally featuring other gym users as visual subjects.
rationale: Subject hierarchy and distracting elements are core composition concerns; privacy is an additional practical reason to check the background.

rule: Open with a shot that establishes the dish or the cook-and-dish relationship, then move to the step that makes the recipe distinctive.
rationale: Wide and medium shots establish context; food creators recommend thinking about the story and planning the shot list.

rule: Use a top-down view when the whole bowl and circular mixing action are clearest from above; use a three-quarter view if hand depth or height matters.
rationale: Canon's food-video creator specifically identifies flatlay as effective for bowl mixing and recommends changing angle to show movement.

rule: Use a closer action shot that preserves the pouring source and landing point in frame.
rationale: Food-video guidance emphasizes texture/action inserts such as piping, drizzling, and garnishing; keeping source and result visible is the compositional translation.

rule: Use side or back/side light and a close view when texture is the message; avoid a flat front-on presentation unless it serves the look.
rationale: A chef-filmmaker recommends side/backlight for dimension and texture; Canon's food creator advises close details.

rule: Give the plated food its own composed hero frame, with enough surrounding context to identify serving or table setting when relevant.
rationale: The food filmmaker advises composing each shot like a still photograph; a wider view can establish dish scale and context.

rule: Use a medium-close or medium frame for the instruction, then insert ingredient and hand-action shots rather than covering every step with the talking head.
rationale: Medium shots retain dialogue and body language; close-ups isolate details. Creator guidance recommends planning angle changes and B-roll.

rule: Place the ingredient list over a calm region of the kitchen or countertop, away from the hands, vessels, and active food.
rationale: Negative space supports readable hierarchy; overlays should not obscure important underlying information.

scenario: Food and creator in the same frame
rule: Keep the face and dish as separate readable focal points; move the dish closer to the lens only if focus and scale remain clear in a test take.
rationale: Product-demonstration advice separates presenter and close product shots; a test avoids assuming that a phone will focus on both distances.

rule: Compose enough of the work surface to show where ingredients enter and where the finished food goes; remove unrelated clutter from that action area.
rationale: Canon recommends planning shot angles and item placement; uncluttered composition improves focus on the subject.

scenario: Food tutorial with fast and slow beats
rule: Use a stable wide or medium action view for process continuity and close inserts for tactile moments; keep each transition purposeful.
rationale: Food creator guidance advocates mixing wide and close angles and using speed changes selectively; Canon advises simple, purposeful transitions.

rule: Show location/context briefly, then prioritize the dish or the person tasting it according to the beat; do not let the background take attention from the featured food.
rationale: Wide/medium shots establish setting while close views feature the subject; food and travel-vlog guidance supports varied coverage.

rule: Use a medium-close talking frame for the explanation and cut to dedicated product-detail footage for ports, buttons, or finish.
rationale: Product videos should demonstrate distinctive features in close-up; talking frame alone may not reveal them.

scenario: Phone or small device held to camera
rule: Keep the device screen oriented to the viewer and large enough to read; record a separate screen capture if the live screen is too small or reflective.
rationale: A product demo should make operation and key features visible. The screen-capture fallback is a practical legibility judgment.

rule: Place the presenter and compared products in clearly separated visual positions, and label each item adjacent to—not over—the feature being evaluated.
rationale: Rule-of-thirds composition can distribute points of interest; readable callouts must not overpower underlying information.

rule: Compose the tabletop so the package opening and emerging item remain visible; use a closer insert when packaging details or included accessories matter.
rationale: Product demos benefit from showing the product in action and close-ups of specifications; table action benefits from a suitable camera angle.

rule: Begin with a wider view that explains the desk arrangement, then use close inserts for the device or accessory being discussed.
rationale: Wide views establish setting; close shots isolate detail. This is a professional shot-size principle applied to tech content.

rule: Keep the screen capture and the creator's face from competing for equal prominence; enlarge whichever carries the current spoken point.
rationale: Composition guides the viewer's eye and product/tutorial annotations should clarify the important content. Exact picture-in-picture proportions are not standardized here.

rule: Show the hands performing the control or function in a clear medium-close view before cutting to a screen/detail insert if needed.
rationale: Product scripts should mark action points; demo videos show functions live and may use close-ups to reveal them.

rule: Keep the CTA distinct from the device demonstration; place it in quiet space or in its own closing beat after the feature is shown.
rationale: Product-video guidance places a call to action at the end; screen annotations should not hide product details.

rule: Reposition the device or camera until reflections no longer conceal the feature; retain a plain background where the product outline is hard to distinguish.
rationale: The goal is visible product function and a clear focal point; product-video advice emphasizes even, consistent lighting and visible features.

rule: Use a close product shot for size and finish, then include a contextual shot showing how it attaches or is used.
rationale: A product demo should show distinguishing details and real use; close and medium/wide views carry different information.

rule: Keep the active application window as the primary visual; zoom or crop to the control currently being described without removing necessary context.
rationale: Screen-recording guidance recommends zooming to clarify details but not so far that context/quality is lost.

rule: Make the cursor path and click target visible; use a restrained highlight when the control would otherwise be hard to find.
rationale: Adobe's demo documentation supports pointer paths and highlight boxes; the rule is directly grounded in software-demo practice.

rule: Put the explanation next to the relevant field only when it does not cover input text; otherwise show the field first and explain in a separate beat.
rationale: Callouts must not cover or overpower on-screen information; their purpose is to clarify key points.

rule: Use a small presenter window only while the face adds context; switch to a screen-dominant view for fine controls or generated output.
rationale: Tutorial hierarchy should follow the information being taught; screen demos need readable controls, while close shots support expressions.

rule: Show input and output with labels and comparable crop/scale; do not place labels on top of the changed feature.
rationale: Comparison requires clear visual correspondence; callouts should not obscure the content they explain.

rule: Capture the app at a readable scale and keep instructional captions in a separate clear area; verify both in the final vertical export.
rationale: Screen overlays and text can obscure controls, and screen-recording zoom is a standard way to preserve legibility.

rule: Let the generated result occupy the visual focus during reveal; place model, prompt, or settings information in a secondary labeled beat.
rationale: Visual hierarchy directs attention; explaining every control simultaneously risks overpowering the result.

scenario: Sensitive user data appears in screen capture
rule: Blur or crop personal data before publishing, while keeping the relevant interface state visible.
rationale: Adobe demo guidance explicitly provides blur areas for privacy in software simulations.

rule: Use captions that do not cover the control or result being narrated; check actual placement in the target app preview.
rationale: Captions should remain readable and production should keep key text out of the lower third; native UI differs by surface.

rule: Break a long operation into clear visual steps and use a purposeful crop/zoom at each key state rather than a continuous tiny full-screen recording.
rationale: Screen-recording instruction endorses zoom for clarity and visual annotations to guide attention; stepwise instructional organization is supported by training-video guidance.

rule: Use a stable chest-up or medium frame for the core explanation, keeping the face and teaching gesture unobstructed.
rationale: Medium-close framing conveys expressions and some body language; educational visuals should remain clear and accessible.

rule: Give the chart a screen-dominant beat; enlarge the relevant region and label the axis/series before adding interpretation text.
rationale: Instructional screen guidance supports zooming to clarify detail; annotations should clarify without overpowering content.

rule: Keep the chart away from the speaker's face and make its visual hierarchy unmistakable; use a cut to full chart if it becomes crowded.
rationale: Composition should guide attention and readable slides/visuals are an accessibility requirement in ASU's teaching guidance.

scenario: Numbers or key terms on screen
rule: Use concise labels adjacent to the item they identify, but not on top of chart values or the presenter's mouth/eyes.
rationale: Callouts should guide and clarify, not cover important screen information; concise accessible text benefits comprehension.

rule: Crop to the relevant cells/metrics and reveal the larger dashboard only when context is needed.
rationale: Screen zoom makes details easier to read; overly tight zoom can reduce context, so sequence detail and overview.

scenario: Educational talking head with a key takeaway
rule: Use a quiet area for the takeaway text and leave captions their own readable space; avoid piling title, subtitles, chart, and UI into one region.
rationale: Accessibility guidance recommends readable captions and moving key on-screen text out of the lower third; annotation guidance cautions against overpowering content.

rule: Place the chart or label on the side toward which the presenter gestures, while ensuring the hand does not obscure the item.
rationale: Composition and pointing action can direct attention; product-video scripts recommend planning action points. Exact side depends on gesture and UI.

rule: Show one main visual idea per beat, then return to the presenter or summary frame to restate the takeaway.
rationale: Training-video guidance calls for clear objectives and step-by-step visuals; this sequencing is practical pedagogy, not a guaranteed engagement result.

rule: Keep required qualification text visible and legible without placing it over critical chart data; give it a dedicated calm frame if necessary.
rationale: Text should not obscure visual information and must remain readable; this is an accessibility and clarity recommendation.

scenario: Showing a calculator or physical document
rule: Use an overhead or oblique close shot for the relevant working area and keep fingers, numbers, and the current step visible together.
rationale: Top-down views are effective for tabletop tutorials; close-ups clarify a detailed process.

rule: Use direct eye contact and a centered or slightly off-center medium-close composition that supports the speaker's delivery.
rationale: Direct lens eyeline signals audience address; center and thirds are both valid choices when intentional.

rule: Allow more negative space or a wider setting only when the visual distance supports the emotional beat; return to a closer frame for detail.
rationale: Negative space can convey isolation, scale, or mood; closer shots increase access to expression.

rule: Leave lead room in the walking direction and avoid placing title text where it masks the path or the speaker's face.
rationale: Leading/looking room implies movement; overlays should not obscure important image content.

rule: Use the landscape as context, but keep the speaker large enough to carry the spoken message on a phone screen.
rationale: Wide shots establish setting, while close and medium shots retain emotional connection; vertical views naturally focus attention on people.

rule: Place the quote in uncluttered negative space, separate from the face and any essential moving background detail.
rationale: Negative space supports focus and text; overlay guidance warns against covering important content.

rule: Use a medium view that includes the purposeful desk action, then isolate a meaningful object in a detail shot rather than leaving unrelated clutter prominent.
rationale: Medium shots show action/context; distractions should be managed and details can be isolated by a close-up.

rule: Keep recurring progress shots visually comparable in viewpoint and framing; use a separate wider shot for context or contrast.
rationale: Comparable framing makes a visual comparison easier to interpret; this is a practical production choice, not a platform rule.

rule: A deliberate lower camera angle may add visual power, but use it selectively and retain a natural, readable face frame.
rationale: Shot-angle guidance associates low angles with anticipation/power; this is an expressive option, not a universal authority cue.

scenario: Call to action at the end
rule: Give the CTA its own uncluttered closing beat, with the speaker or relevant next step clearly visible and text checked against app controls.
rationale: Product-video guidance places a CTA at the end; platform previews are necessary because UI overlays are surface-dependent.

rule: Establish the place with a wider scene, then move to a human-scale view or detail that explains why the location matters to the story.
rationale: Wide shots establish a setting; travel vlogging covers diverse scenes and benefits from varied planned footage.

rule: Keep face and useful location context in view while walking; use stabilization or pause for a detail shot rather than allowing shake to obscure the scene.
rationale: Vlog guidance describes on-the-go capture and stabilization; portrait framing should prioritize the person and relevant context.

rule: Leave room for the subject's path and confirm both entry and exit positions before recording.
rationale: Lead room supports movement direction; shot planning and movement checks are practical scene-coverage habits.

rule: Show enough foreground to explain the action and include a cutaway to the destination or result when POV alone lacks context.
rationale: POV shots can convey involvement; establishing and detail shots communicate context that an isolated view may not.

rule: Choose either the person or landmark as the primary subject for each shot; use scale and negative space to support the secondary one.
rationale: Negative space can establish scale; wide shots show a person's relation to the environment.

rule: Reposition or tighten the frame to separate the featured person/food/object from distracting motion in the background.
rationale: Cinematography guidance warns about moving distractions through windows/backgrounds; composition advice recommends removing distracting elements.

scenario: Travel creator at a window or viewpoint
rule: Place the creator where the outside view remains identifiable but does not overpower the face; check exposure and reflection in a test frame.
rationale: Window backgrounds can provide light/context but traffic and competing views may distract; the balance depends on actual scene.

rule: Show the maker/action and its result in complementary views; use a close detail for texture and a wider view for place/context.
rationale: Food-video advice recommends switching flatlay, three-quarter, close, and wide views; wide shots establish location.

rule: Keep the place label brief and position it in clear space, not over a face, landmark identifier, or key activity.
rationale: Negative space carries labels while preserving focal content; accessibility guidance prioritizes legibility.

rule: Choose each insert for a distinct visual detail and maintain purposeful transitions rather than repeating near-identical views.
rationale: Canon social-video education recommends simple, purposeful transitions; varied planned shots give each beat a role.

rule: Use an off-camera eyeline toward the interviewer for a conversational interview; use direct lens gaze when the person addresses viewers.
rationale: Professional cinematography explicitly distinguishes interview eyeline from direct audience address.

scenario: Interviewee on one side of frame
rule: Leave looking room in front of the interviewee's eyeline and use the opposite space only for a simple title or visual aid.
rationale: Lead/look room is an established composition principle; text should not compete with face or essential content.

rule: Use a two-shot that keeps both faces readable when their exchange is the point; cut to a single when a response or reaction becomes the focus.
rationale: Medium framing supports group interaction; singles clarify individual emotional responses.

scenario: Two speakers recorded in separate clips
rule: Keep both eyelines oriented consistently to preserve the sense of conversational direction; avoid accidentally reversing the established screen relationship.
rationale: ASC interview guidance recommends maintaining the same side of the eyeline/180-degree line across cameras for continuity.

scenario: Podcast excerpt with host and guest
rule: Favor the active speaker while retaining a reaction view when the response adds meaning; avoid a tiny equal split if neither face is legible.
rationale: Shot size and composition should guide attention; tighter singles and wider context views serve different purposes.

rule: Arrange heads at distinct, non-overlapping positions and increase camera distance or use an intentional stacked composition until every participant is recognizable.
rationale: Composition should maintain visual separation and readable subjects; vertical group layout is a practical adaptation, not a universal layout prescription.

rule: Reserve readable caption space that does not cover any speaker's face; test captions against the final platform interface.
rationale: Section 508 says key on-screen text should be kept out of the lower third and captions remain readable; app UI may vary.

rule: Frame each remote participant at a similar visual scale when showing them together, or cut between clear individual views instead of shrinking faces excessively.
rationale: Medium framing supports dialogue and group interaction; this is a readability-focused practical recommendation.

rule: Move the subject away from the wall when possible and angle the camera to reveal useful depth; keep background objects from intersecting the head or face.
rationale: ASC guidance says subjects directly against walls/corners look flat and recommends angled walls/leading lines while avoiding busy backgrounds.

rule: Use alternate shot sizes or angles for edit points while keeping both cameras on the established side of the interview eyeline.
rationale: ASC interview guidance discusses multiple perspectives and keeping cameras on the same side of the 180-degree line.

rule: Keep the face and gesture in a clear medium-close frame; leave room for a reaction beat rather than filling the frame with explanatory text.
rationale: Close/medium-close shots reveal expression and body language; visual clutter competes with the intended focal point.

rule: Establish who is where before the exchange, then use a clear single or reaction view when the joke depends on a specific response.
rationale: Wide/medium shots orient the audience; close-ups highlight emotion and reactions.

rule: Keep the full action path and prop visible from setup through payoff; do not crop the object needed to understand the joke.
rationale: Shot choice should show the significant action and relevant object; a wider view can preserve spatial context.

rule: Hold a stable composition through the reaction long enough for the expression to read; do not add a competing text effect at the same moment.
rationale: Close-ups convey emotion; excessive effects can distract from meaning. Exact timing remains editorial judgment.

rule: Use a mix of context and detail shots, keeping recurring actions visually clear and the background relevant to the story.
rationale: Vlog guidance supports varied subject/environment coverage; shot-size principles distinguish location from detail.

rule: Choose either the creator's face or the POV event as the main visual for each beat; cut or reframe when the audience must see both.
rationale: A clear visual hierarchy guides attention; close/POV shots carry distinct kinds of information.

rule: Keep the face separate from the referenced image and place labels only in unused regions of the composite; check edge visibility on the final export.
rationale: Creator education recognizes green screen; composition and overlay guidance require that text clarify without covering the visual reference.

rule: Show a product only when it contributes to the action or story; give it a clean detail insert if viewers need to identify it.
rationale: Product-video guidance uses close-ups to demonstrate features, while composition requires a clear focal hierarchy.

rule: Keep the setup text concise and visually separate from the face/action; make the punchline readable without hiding the reveal.
rationale: Readable text and uncluttered visual hierarchy improve clarity; annotations must not overshadow the image.

rule: Mark a consistent subject landing point for each take so the transition reads cleanly; use a different frame only when the change itself is the joke.
rationale: Purposeful consistent transitions are recommended by creator education; matching landing position is a practical production judgment.
